description:
How fast is Nvidia's cut-price ray tracing GPU, the RTX 2060? Can it match or beat GTX 1070 Ti or even GTX 1080? And if the hardware has been downgraded for mainstream budgets, are the ray tracing features actually useful - in short, how well does it run Battlefield 5 RTX? In this detailed review, you'll get all the benches you'll need, you'll see Turing VRS technology analysed - and yes, you'll get to see BF5 running with RT enabled on the new hardware.

Check out our deep dive into variable rate shading: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edYiCE0b8-c

comments.text: DLSS currently has no perfect implementation. Metro's implementation at least achieves a resolution upscale that is higher than the native render target, but it still isn't as good as it could get. Neural networks are really, really good at image processing. There are even instances where a neural network is given a random persons face, you can then partially or fully erase something like the persons eye, mouth, nose...etc and it will reconstruct the missing details, to the point that you would be hard pressed to tell that the imagine is reconstructed. Of course that is a very specifically trained neural network where a face has a more limited solution space. However, in the case of DLSS, it has a lot more information, all of the neighboring pixel information for upscaling. In theory, a properly trained neural network can achieve the same scaling image quality with a better performance ratio, than a regular super sampled image that is then down sampled (which can produce it's own artifacts). In theory, it can achieve more temporally stable reconstruction than checkerboard rendering and maintain it's full resolution with any amount of motion. "In theory" is the key phrase there though. I don't have the specifics of the neural network structure of DLSS, nor do I have any specifics on their exact training methodology. BFV's implementation seems to be pretty poor, Metro's seems to be at least better than native, but still not living up to the promise of "4k" equivalence. With that said, the tech and theory is very sound and definitely has the potential to be a lot better overall compared to any other existing method. With that said, if the end result is a 4k output, the implementations should be able to render HUD (text and graphical GUI elements) at native 4k and only use DLSS for the actual render targets, so text, if implemented correctly, shouldn't be a factor. Supposedly if a game engine supports TAA, then it can support DLSS, if so then that hints that DLSS runs later in the render pipeline after everything has been rendered overall, but before HUD elements (you don't want HUD elements being processed by a TAA implementation). If you're thinking it's limited to text, you're drastically misunderstanding he tech's application.

The way I see it is like this, anyone old enough to remember when 3d accelerators " more like decelerators" first came out? The performance was usually far worse than just using software rendering. Now Ray tracing is just coming out we're seeing something similar, but instead of software vs 3d accelerated, we're seeing "normal" 3d acceleration vs ray traced, where Ray tracing takes a huge hit into the performance. comments.text:
Yup, remember it well.
My first rasterizer was Verite 2200 it had amazing image quality, but my CPU was bottleneck and framerates didn't really improve. (I could render fullscreen and higher resolution though.)

Difference is that in during early days we had software rasterization -> hardware rasterization and now we are moving to rasterization + ray-tracing.
There is a lot of additional work that goes into raytracing before rays are actually traced and more after intersections have happened. (BVH generation etc.)

Would love to see benchmarks which would do all the extra work needed before tracing and actually skip the tracing and shading needed.
Also no game uses DXR fallback layer and show us how fast the raytracing and additional shading would be using compute. (How much does possible additional caches in RT unit help and how much intersection work frees ALUs for actual shading.)

There should be interesting uses for RT cores outside the obvious, things like per pixel shader selection have been heard. (Should be fun for all sort of texture space work as well.)

comments.text: That way of thinking has changed in the last few years. Main problem is that the entire chip foundry industry has been finding it harder and harder to achieve the next node in the photolithography process shrink schedule. If you notice, AMD, Intel on the CPU side have stagnated a bit (with only adding more cores, with the expected increase in die area used), and Nvidia and AMD both have stagnated in terms of performance increases, instead relying on architectural improvements. In the past, the process shrinks came on schedule and gave a way for each foundry to improve performance while still using less die area, which also lead to lower prices. As the process shrinks became harder and more expensive to achieve, the prices have stagnated or even increased, while performance improvements have been (relatively speaking) minor. Don't get me wrong, process shrinks are still happening, with a few foundries going smaller soon (if their process releases are to be believed). However, you'll start to see more of a push on the technology on that die area and general architectural improvements instead of just a raw speed improvement. Even if we magically get an easy pass on the next couple of nodes... we're in general approaching the limits of silicon itself. In other words, we're getting pretty close to hitting a wall in our existing tech. Material sciences are my bet for future increases in the next 10+ years. Propagation delay and energy wastage might be improved by better materials, allowing higher clocks even if we have to step back and increase our transistor feature size.

comments.author: @JimBob1937

comments.text: ​ @gamerxt333  Case in point, the reflections (just a single part of ray tracing) has been severely limited until now. You either used screen space reflections which have obvious limitations. Or you can use geometry doubling, mirroring the geometry on the other side of content that is suppose to be reflective. Or you can use a render to texture, which requires a secondary camera to render out a frame to texture and use that texture as the reflection. The SSR are bad but fast. The geometry doubling is limited to static elements (or a single character mirrored across the geometry) and doesn't scale to more complex and dynamic scenes. The render to texture can be fairly effective but is very heavy on performance and requires the entire scene and all effect buffers to be rendered for just that reflection for every frame of that geometry and the result is only useful for the render to texture camera's relative position to the player, so it may not scale well if you want or need to have a lot of accurate reflective surfaces (would require more and more render to texture camera's). Performance can be improved on the latter technique by having the render to texture target only update periodically, which can work but isn't ideal. All of these take a fair amount of effort to setup, test, tweak, and maintain. Hence, the universal and accurate approach of ray tracing... and that's just the reflection component. Technically you still have things like cube mapping and other environmental mapping techniques, but I don't think those would be fair to compare against since they don't produce accurate dynamic reflections. You may not realize it, but your games are being severely limited in quite a few areas by the limitations of this fakery.

comments.text: @wile123456 , it's like a much more advanced version of checkerboard rendering. Checkerboard rendering requires multiple frames to not have a checkered resolution separation effect and is more similar to interlacing with a de-interlacing filter on the final display. However, DLSS is effectively training a neural network given a 1440p frame what a 4k frame should look like. Obviously since the convolutional neural network/CNN (so I assume) is effectively filling in missing data, it won't be perfect compared to a true 4k render (that would be magical), it can create a rather impressive resolution upscale essentially that doesn't have a reliance on temporal data. They may enhance it with that, not sure, but it's not required. Compared to checkerboard rendering, which is basically averaging even and odd pixel rendering, which will look good stationary but turn blurrier with movement, the CNN output should be fairly stable in both scenarios. It's basically a giant improvement on the idea of checkerboard rendering in just about every fashion. My guess is that they're merely exporting out the trained data biases and weights and applying them on a per application basis, with different games (and maybe even levels) having different training sets.
